citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.location: p. 683 (PDF p. 11); proof in Supplement A, Section 4, pp. 6–7
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 1. For every sequence of experimental designs, if Assumption 2 does not hold, there exists a sequence of potential outcomes satisfying Assumption 1 such that the HT and HÁ estimators do not converge in probability to EATE. [Reading, from the proof] Given a sequence of designs satisfying Assumption 1A and a sequence $(d_{\mathrm{AVG}})$ with $\limsup_{n \to \infty} n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}} > 0$, there are potential outcomes, satisfying Assumptions 1B and 1C and with $\limsup_{n \to \infty} n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$ unchanged, for which neither $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ nor $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ converges in probability to zero.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement A, pp. 6–7] For a fixed $n$, a design satisfying Assumption 1A with constant $k$, a number $\lambda \in (0, 1]$, $M = \lceil\lambda^{0.5}n\rceil$, and the potential outcomes $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = n M^{-1} z_1\left[z_i\Pr(Z_i = 1) - (1 - z_i)\Pr(Z_i = 0)\right]$ if $i \le M$ and $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ otherwise: (a) $d_{ij} = 1$ if $i = j$ or $i, j \le M$, and 0 otherwise; (b) $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{M^2}{n} + \frac{n - M}{n} \ge \lambda n$; (c) $|y_i(\mathbf{z})| \le n M^{-1}[\Pr(Z_i = 1) + \Pr(Z_i = 0)] \le \lambda^{-0.5}$; (d) $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \Pr(Z_1 = 1)$; (e) $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = Z_1$; (f) $|\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}| = |Z_1 - \Pr(Z_1 = 1)| \ge k^{-1}$ with probability one; (g) on $\{Z_1 = 0\}$ every observed outcome is zero, so $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = 0$ wherever it is defined, and $\Pr(|\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}| \ge k^{-1}) \ge \Pr(Z_1 = 0) \ge k^{-1}$ (the paper says only that the proof for the Hájek estimator follows the same structure). The selection of infinitely many $n$ at which these outcomes are used is the step corrected under P009-E014: for $L = \limsup n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}} > 0$ and $0 < c < L$, the set $\{n : d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \ge cn\}$ is infinite.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H2; it held up, with the caveat that one line of the printed proof is false as written (P009-E014, an error rated Minor; the counterexample and corrected step are separate targets). The proposition is an existence statement about sequences. The Hájek estimator is undefined when a treatment arm is empty (clarity note P009-E015); item (g) is stated on the event where it is defined.

canonical_claim.location: p. 684 (PDF p. 12); proof in Supplement A, Section 5, pp. 7–9
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 2. With a Bernoulli randomization design under restricted interference (Assumption 2), the HT and HÁ estimators are consistent for EATE and converge at the following rates: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$. [Standing hypothesis: Assumption 1, with the weakest exponents $q = 2$ and $s = 1$ sufficing (p. 682).]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Definition A1 and Corollary A1: Supplement A, p. 2] DEFINITION A1. $\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})]$, $\breve\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = z]$, $\hat\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]Y_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$, $\hat n_z = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$. COROLLARY A1. $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mu_1 - \mu_0$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \breve\mu_1 - \breve\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = (\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1) - (\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1\right) - \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0\right)$. [Lemmas used to pass from exact moments to rates: Supplement A] LEMMA A1 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_z] = \breve\mu_z$. LEMMA A2 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat n_z] = n$. LEMMA A5 (p. 4). If the rate of convergence in the $L_2$-norm for a sequence of random variables is govern by a sequence $(a_n)$, then the rate of convergence in probability is govern by $(a_n)$ [that is, in the notation of its proof, $\sqrt{\mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]} = \mathcal{O}(a_n)$ implies $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$; the proof is Markov's inequality, $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]/(\kappa^2 a_n^2)$]. LEMMA A6 (p. 4). If $\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = o_p(1)$ and $\hat n_z/n - 1 = o_p(1)$, then: $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p\left((\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z) + (\hat n_z/n - 1)\right)$ [read with the magnitudes of the two errors, clarity note P009-E011; its proof rests on the exact identity $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \frac{\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n} - \frac{(\hat n_z/n - 1)\breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n}$ and on $|\breve\mu_z| \le k^2$].
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement A, pp. 3 and 7–9] For each fixed $n$, under a Bernoulli design and Assumption 1 with constant $k$: (a) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_z] = \breve\mu_z$ (Lemma A1) and $\mathrm{E}[\hat n_z] = n$ (Lemma A2); (b) $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (Lemma A8), so $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = (\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1) - (\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0)$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1\right) - \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0\right)$ (Corollary A1); (c) $(1 - d_{ij})\mathrm{Cov}\left(\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]Y_i, \mathbb{1}[Z_j = z]Y_j\right) = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_z) \le k^4 n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$ (proof of Lemma A9, p. 8, with the first step corrected as in P009-E009); (d) $\mathrm{Var}(\hat n_z/n) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - \Pr(Z_i = z)}{\Pr(Z_i = z)} \le k n^{-1}$ (proof of Lemma A10, p. 8); (e) $|\breve\mu_z| \le k^2$ and the identity of Lemma A6. Consequently $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})^2] \le 4k^4 n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$ for every $n$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H3; it held up, with the caveat that the first inequality in the proof of Lemma A9 is false as printed and is repaired without changing the bound (P009-E009). Lemma A9 (p. 7): under Bernoulli randomization, $\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$; Lemma A10 (p. 8): under Bernoulli randomization and Assumption 2, $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$. The rate statement for the HT estimator needs no Assumption 2; consistency does. The Hájek estimator needs a convention on the vanishing probability event of an empty arm (clarity note P009-E015).

canonical_claim.location: p. 685 (PDF p. 13); proof in Supplement A, Section 6, pp. 9–16
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 3. With a complete randomization design under restricted interference (Assumption 2) and $C_1 = o(n^{0.5})$, the HT and HÁ estimators are consistent for EATE and converge at the following rates: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}C_1)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}C_1)$. [Standing hypothesis: Assumption 1.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Definition A1 and Corollary A1: Supplement A, p. 2] DEFINITION A1. $\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})]$, $\breve\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = z]$, $\hat\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]Y_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$, $\hat n_z = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$. COROLLARY A1. $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mu_1 - \mu_0$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \breve\mu_1 - \breve\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = (\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1) - (\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1\right) - \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0\right)$. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$. [Definitions A2 and A3: Supplement A, p. 9] DEFINITION A2. Let $m = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i$ be the element sum of $\mathbf{Z}$ (i.e., the number of treated units). REMARK. Complete randomization implies that $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ with probability one for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. DEFINITION A3. Let $\reflectbox{c}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ji}$ be the number of units interfering with unit $i$. (The paper prints this symbol as a reflected italic $c$; it is written $\reflectbox{c}_i$ here.) [Lemmas used to pass from exact moments to rates: Supplement A] LEMMA A1 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_z] = \breve\mu_z$. LEMMA A2 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat n_z] = n$. LEMMA A5 (p. 4). If the rate of convergence in the $L_2$-norm for a sequence of random variables is govern by a sequence $(a_n)$, then the rate of convergence in probability is govern by $(a_n)$ [that is, in the notation of its proof, $\sqrt{\mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]} = \mathcal{O}(a_n)$ implies $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$; the proof is Markov's inequality, $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]/(\kappa^2 a_n^2)$]. LEMMA A6 (p. 4). If $\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = o_p(1)$ and $\hat n_z/n - 1 = o_p(1)$, then: $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p\left((\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z) + (\hat n_z/n - 1)\right)$ [read with the magnitudes of the two errors, clarity note P009-E011; its proof rests on the exact identity $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \frac{\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n} - \frac{(\hat n_z/n - 1)\breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n}$ and on $|\breve\mu_z| \le k^2$].
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement A, pp. 9–16] For each fixed $n$, under complete randomization with $m$ treated units and Assumption 1 with constant $k$, writing $T_{\mathrm{MIN}} = \min(m, n - m)$: (a) LEMMA A11. $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\reflectbox{c}_i = C_1$. canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 4. With a paired randomization design under restricted interference, restricted pair-induced interference and pair separation (Assumptions 2, 3 and 4), the HT and HÁ estimators are consistent for EATE and converge at the following rates: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}e_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-1}R_{\mathrm{SUM}})$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}e_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-1}R_{\mathrm{SUM}})$. [Standing hypothesis: Assumption 1.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'.
